clues.q: Often called the "Bard of Avon", this English playwright wrote Hamlet, Macbeth and Romeo and Juliet.
Samuel Langhorne Clemens wrote under this pen name; William Faulkner called him "the father of American literature".
Regarded by many as the greatest novelist of the Victorian era, this English writer created David Copperfield and Ebenezer Scrooge.
Joanne is the real first name of this British author, best known for a seven-book fantasy series about a boy wizard.
This Danish writer is best remembered for 156 literary fairy tales, including The Snow Queen and The Emperor's New Clothes.
This English philologist and Oxford professor of Anglo-Saxon wrote The Silmarillion and created Middle-earth.
clues.a: Who is J. R. R. Tolkien?

clues.q: This American writer known for tales of mystery and the macabre wrote The Raven and The Tell-Tale Heart.
This English writer's six novels, including Emma and Sense and Sensibility, comment on the English landed gentry of the late 18th century.
This pen name was used by Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, an English mathematician who wrote the poem Jabberwocky.
This British author and lay theologian, who taught at both Oxford and Cambridge, wrote The Chronicles of Narnia.
This English author of 66 detective novels wrote Murder on the Orient Express and Death on the Nile.
This British writer and physician created the detective Sherlock Holmes and his assistant Dr. Watson.
This French novelist's Voyages extraordinaires include A Journey to the Centre of the Earth and The Mysterious Island.
Known for horror fiction, this American author of about 200 short stories wrote It, The Shining and Carrie.
This Scottish novelist and travel writer wrote Kidnapped and the poetry collection A Child's Garden of Verses.
No writings survive by this ancient Greek storyteller, yet countless fables have been credited to him.
Born in British India, this English writer created Mowgli and the Just So Stories.
This English novelist wrote The Last Man and an 1818 Gothic novel considered an early example of science fiction.
Eric Arthur Blair used this pen name for works opposing totalitarianism, including Homage to Catalonia.
This American poet often wrote about rural life in New England; his collections include North of Boston and New Hampshire.
Known for an economical, understated style, this American novelist wrote A Farewell to Arms and The Sun Also Rises.
Largely unpublished and unknown during her lifetime, this American poet from Amherst is now considered canonical.
This Russian count, born Lev Nikolayevich, wrote the novels Resurrection and The Kreutzer Sonata.
This French Romantic poet, playwright and politician wrote the novels The Man Who Laughs and Ninety-Three.
Often called the greatest writer in the Spanish language, he wrote the Exemplary Novels and a two-part work considered the first modern novel.
This French novelist wrote Twenty Years After with help from his ghostwriter Auguste Maquet.
This Irish author and playwright wrote The Importance of Being Earnest and The Canterville Ghost.
This English writer of more than forty novels wrote The Time Machine and The Invisible Man.
This American novelist, one of the first to earn a large fortune from writing, wrote White Fang and The Sea-Wolf.
This American, winner of the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature, wrote East of Eden.
This American poet and civil rights activist wrote seven autobiographies, including I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.
This American poet wrote Leaves of Grass and O Captain! My Captain!
This English writer, journalist and spy wrote Moll Flanders and A Journal of the Plague Year.
This Anglo-Irish satirist and cleric created the fictional island of Lilliput and wrote A Modest Proposal.
This English novelist, the elder sister of Emily and Anne, published Jane Eyre under the pseudonym Currer Bell.
Writing as Ellis Bell, this English author published her only novel, about Heathcliff, in 1847.
This American Renaissance writer wrote Typee and the novella Billy Budd, Sailor.
This French writer and aviator from Lyon wrote Night Flight and Wind, Sand and Stars.
This Italian poet's Comedy was later called "Divine" by Giovanni Boccaccio.
This English humourist's most famous work began in 1978 as a BBC radio comedy and grew into a "trilogy of five books".
Regarded as one of the greatest novelists in world literature, this Russian wrote The Idiot and Demons.
This German-language Jewish writer from Prague wrote The Castle and Lost in America.
This Roman poet of the Augustan period wrote the Eclogues, the Georgics and the epic Aeneid.
Called the "father of English literature", this poet and civil servant wrote Troilus and Criseyde.
This English poet and polemicist wrote Areopagitica and a 1667 epic poem about the fall of man.
This 6th Baron and major Romantic poet wrote the long narrative poems Don Juan and Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.
This Russian playwright and physician wrote The Seagull, Uncle Vanya and The Cherry Orchard.
This German polymath, widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language, wrote the poem The Sorcerer's Apprentice.
This English modernist who pioneered stream of consciousness narration wrote Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse.
This Irish modernist wrote Dubliners, Finnegans Wake and A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.
This ancient Greek tragedian wrote more than 120 plays, including Antigone and Electra.
This Roman poet in the reign of Augustus wrote the Metamorphoses and was later exiled to the Black Sea coast.
This modernist poet and 1948 Nobel laureate wrote The Waste Land and The Hollow Men.
This second-generation English Romantic poet died of tuberculosis at just 25.
This English Romantic poet published Lyrical Ballads with Samuel Taylor Coleridge; his magnum opus is The Prelude.
This American novelist and 1993 Nobel laureate wrote The Bluest Eye, Song of Solomon and Beloved.
Known affectionately as Gabo, this Colombian writer wrote Love in the Time of Cholera.
This biochemistry professor, one of science fiction's "Big Three", wrote I, Robot and the Foundation series.
This English writer and philosopher wrote The Doors of Perception and The Perennial Philosophy.
This Scottish novelist known for his Waverley novels wrote Ivanhoe and Rob Roy.
Considered the founder of modern Russian literature, this poet wrote The Captain's Daughter and Boris Godunov.
Jean-Baptiste Poquelin used this stage name; he wrote the comedies Tartuffe and The Miser.
Called "the father of modern drama", this Norwegian playwright wrote A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler.
This French novelist, a leading exponent of literary realism, wrote Sentimental Education and Salammbo.
This French philosopher, the first literature Nobel laureate born in Africa, wrote The Plague and The Myth of Sisyphus.
This English Romantic poet, husband of the author of Frankenstein, wrote Ozymandias.
This English poet, painter and printmaker created Songs of Innocence and of Experience.
Mary Ann Evans used this pen name for novels including Middlemarch and Silas Marner.
This American transcendentalist wrote Walden and the essay Civil Disobedience.
This American essayist and poet led the transcendentalist movement of the mid-19th century and wrote the Concord Hymn.
Along with Aeschylus and Sophocles, this tragedian of classical Athens wrote Medea and The Trojan Women.
This Irish playwright who wrote in both English and French wrote Endgame and Krapp's Last Tape.
This Russian poet's first book of poems was My Sister, Life; his novel about Yuri Zhivago was refused publication in the USSR.
This Soviet dissident and 1970 Nobel laureate wrote The Gulag Archipelago.
This Italian medievalist and semiotician wrote Foucault's Pendulum.
This Polish-British novelist, who did not speak English fluently until his twenties, wrote Lord Jim and Nostromo.
This American writer set many stories in fictional Yoknapatawpha County, Mississippi, and wrote As I Lay Dying.
This ancient Greek lyric poet from the island of Lesbos was called the "Tenth Muse".
This Irish playwright, who preferred to be known without his first name, wrote Pygmalion and Saint Joan.
This best-selling Japanese writer wrote Norwegian Wood, Kafka on the Shore and 1Q84.
This Japanese novelist and lady-in-waiting of the Heian period wrote The Tale of Genji.
The most famous Japanese poet of the Edo period, he wrote Oku no Hosomichi and the Frog Poem.
Also known by the courtesy name Taibai, this Tang dynasty poet wrote Quiet Night Thought.
In 1913 this Bengali poet, author of Gitanjali, became the first non-European to win a Nobel Prize in Literature.
This Egyptian writer of the Cairo Trilogy and Midaq Alley won the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature.
This French novelist's magnum opus is La Comedie humaine; it includes Pere Goriot and Eugenie Grandet.
The best-known practitioner of naturalism, this French novelist wrote the open letter J'accuse...!
Marie-Henri Beyle used this pen name; he wrote The Red and the Black and The Charterhouse of Parma.
This Russian writer of Ukrainian origin wrote The Nose, The Overcoat and The Government Inspector.
This Russian novelist's first major publication was A Sportsman's Sketches; he later wrote Fathers and Sons.
This Argentine short-story writer's best-known works are Ficciones and El Aleph.
This French novelist's seven-volume masterpiece, published from 1913 to 1927, totals about 1.25 million words.
This Chilean poet-diplomat and 1971 Nobel laureate wrote Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair.
This Persian lyric poet from Shiraz is so beloved that many Iranians learn his poems by heart.
This Persian poet wrote the Shahnameh, one of the world's longest epic poems by a single poet.
This German novelist and 1929 Nobel laureate wrote Buddenbrooks, Death in Venice and The Magic Mountain.
This Austrian poet wrote the Duino Elegies and the Sonnets to Orpheus.
In 1909 this Swedish author of The Wonderful Adventures of Nils became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
This Italian scholar and poet, an early Renaissance humanist, is credited with rediscovering Cicero's letters.
This Spanish poet of the Generation of '27 wrote the plays Blood Wedding and The House of Bernarda Alba.
Who is this playwright from Stratford-upon-Avon, author of 'Romeo and Juliet'?
Who is this author of 'The Adventures of Tom Sawyer', who wrote under a pen name?
Who is this author, whose seven fantasy novels follow a boy wizard at Hogwarts?
Who is this author, who wrote 'The Cat in the Hat' and 'Green Eggs and Ham'?
Who is this Victorian novelist, author of 'Oliver Twist' and 'A Christmas Carol'?
Who is this author of 'Pride and Prejudice', shown in a sketch by her sister Cassandra?
Who is this writer of 'The Raven' and 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?

clues.q: Who is this author in the photo, who wrote 'The Old Man and the Sea'?
Who is this reclusive poet from Amherst, Massachusetts, who wrote 'Because I could not stop for Death'?
Who is this Russian novelist, author of 'War and Peace' and 'Anna Karenina'?
Who is this Jazz Age author, who wrote 'The Great Gatsby'?
Who is this Alabama author, whose 1960 novel 'To Kill a Mockingbird' won the Pulitzer Prize?
Who is this Irish wit, author of 'The Picture of Dorian Gray' and 'The Importance of Being Earnest'?
Who is this Prague-born writer, whose character Gregor Samsa wakes up as an insect?
Who is this Russian author of 'Crime and Punishment'?
Who is this author of 'Moby-Dick', shown in an 1870 portrait?
Who is this Spanish writer, who lost the use of his left hand at Lepanto and wrote about a deluded knight?
Who is this Harlem Renaissance author of 'Their Eyes Were Watching God'?
Who is this Bengali poet, the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1913?
Listen: this 1890 wax-cylinder recording is believed to be which poet reading his poem 'America'?
